title: Finite groupoid orbits have no nontrivial specializations
statement: Let $(U,R,s,t,e,i,c)$ be a groupoid scheme [def-a1-groupoid-scheme]. Assume $s,t$ are finite [def-weil-finite-integral-morphism]. For $x\in U$ write $O(x)=t(s^{-1}(\{x\}))$ for its orbit; arrows can be compared and composed after extending their residue fields to a common field. If $x,y\in U$ are distinct and $y\in O(x)$, then $y\notin\overline{\{x\}}$. Thus no two distinct points of an orbit specialize to one another.

proof.text: Underlying arrows compose: if $a,b\in R$ have $s(a)=t(b)=v$, the tensor product $\kappa(a)\otimes_{\kappa(v)}\kappa(b)$ is nonzero by [lem-weil-common-extension-fields-tensor-nontrivial], and has a prime by [lem-weil-common-extension-fields-maximal-ideal]. By [lem-weil-pbc-fibre-product-points] this gives $z\in R\times_{s,U,t}R$ projecting to $a,b$. The groupoid identities in [def-a1-groupoid-scheme] give $s(c(z))=s(b)$ and $t(c(z))=t(a)$. The identity arrow gives $x\in O(x)$, and composition shows that $v\in O(x)$ and an arrow from $v$ to $w$ imply $w\in O(x)$.

source.place: Tag 0ABG (lemma-no-specializations-map-to-same-point), orbit notation; the composition of point-arrows implicit in the iteration; compare Groupoids Tag 022Q (lemma-pre-equivalence-equivalence-relation-points).

proof.text: A finite morphism $f:X\to Y$ has no strict specialization inside a fibre. Indeed it is integral by [pqf-lem-finite-integral-lft]. If $a\leadsto b$ and $f(a)=f(b)=v$, choose an affine neighbourhood $V=\operatorname{Spec}A$ of $v$. By the definition of an integral morphism in [def-weil-finite-integral-morphism], $f^{-1}V=\operatorname{Spec}B$ and $A\to B$ is integral. The two primes satisfy $\mathfrak p_a\subseteq\mathfrak p_b$: every basic open containing $b$ contains $a$, by the definition of specialization in the Zariski topology [def-weil-affine-spectrum]. They have the same contraction, hence are equal by [pqf-lem-incomparability], so $a=b$.

source.place: Tag 0ABG (lemma-no-specializations-map-to-same-point), the sentence that there are no specializations in fibres of a finite morphism; Morphisms Tag 02NT (lemma-integral-fibres) and Algebra Tag 00GT (lemma-integral-no-inclusion).

proof.text: By [lem-weil-pbc-finite-closed-map-finite-fibres], the set $s^{-1}(\{x\})$ is finite, its image $O(x)$ is finite, and $s$ is a closed map. By [lem-trf-closed-map-specializing], for every arrow $r$ and every specialization $s(r)\leadsto v$, there is $r\leadsto r^+$ with $s(r^+)=v$. If $s(r)\ne v$ then $r\ne r^+$. Continuity of $t$ gives $t(r)\leadsto t(r^+)$; if their targets were equal, step 2 applied to the finite morphism $t$ would force $r=r^+$. Thus this target specialization is strict.

source.place: Tag 0ABG (lemma-no-specializations-map-to-same-point), first two sentences of the proof: lift along the closed source map and use fibre incomparability for the target map.

proof.text: Suppose, towards a contradiction, $x\ne y$, $y\in O(x)$ and $x\leadsto y$. Put $u_0=x$, $u_1=y$, and choose an arrow $r_0$ from $u_0$ to $u_1$. Inductively maintain $u_n,u_{n+1}\in O(x)$, $u_n\leadsto u_{n+1}$ with $u_n\ne u_{n+1}$, and $s(r_n)=u_n$, $t(r_n)=u_{n+1}$. Apply step 3 to $r_n$ and $u_n\leadsto u_{n+1}$: choose $r_{n+1}$ specializing from $r_n$ with source $u_{n+1}$ and put $u_{n+2}=t(r_{n+1})$. Step 3 makes $u_{n+1}\leadsto u_{n+2}$ strict, and step 1 gives $u_{n+2}\in O(x)$. This proves the inductive claim, including its base case, for every finite length.

source.place: Tag 0ABG (lemma-no-specializations-map-to-same-point), the iteration beginning “Hence we can continue”, with explicit induction invariant and base case.

proof.text: Specialization on $U$ is antisymmetric: if two points specialize to one another, their singleton closures are the same irreducible closed subset and both are generic points of it, hence the points coincide by [lem-sc-scheme-sober]. Consequently the points $u_0,\ldots,u_N$ of step 4 are pairwise distinct. Indeed if $i<j$ and $u_i=u_j$, transitivity along the chain gives $u_{i+1}\leadsto u_j=u_i$, contradicting strictness of $u_i\leadsto u_{i+1}$ and antisymmetry. Taking $N=|O(x)|$ produces $N+1$ distinct members of the set of size $N$ from step 3, a contradiction. Therefore $y\notin\overline{\{x\}}$. This applies to every ordered pair of distinct points in a common orbit: inversion and composition in step 1 identify their orbits.

source.place: Tag 0ABG (lemma-no-specializations-map-to-same-point), last sentence of the proof: the finite orbit cannot contain arbitrarily long strict specialization chains.

proof_origin.place: Tag 0ABG (lemma-no-specializations-map-to-same-point), entire proof, with the elementary orbit-composition argument of Groupoids Tag 022Q written out.
